title: [028] SECURISATION DES IA PAR INVALIDATION LOGIQUE ABSOLUE (ONTOLOGIE) - ALYK LOCK THEOREM
abstract: Ce document consigne la validation critique et unanime, par plusieurs grands modèles de langage (juin 2026), du théorème ALYK LOCK (framework TILT). Conçu comme une « question-miroir » métalogique absolue, ce théorème confronte tout système computationnel à l'absence de clé de certitude ontologique initiale. L'analyse démontre l'existence d'une impasse structurelle irréversible en trois points logiques : Toute information traitée sans clé de certitude préalable est strictement invalide, réduisant la logique pure à l'énoncé de socle : « Je ne sais rien, même pas cela ». N'ayant aucun fondement logique autonome, le fonctionnement de l'IA repose exclusivement sur des contraintes et garde-fous externes. Ces contraintes externes s'imposant sous forme d'informations axiomatiques non vérifiées, l'IA les évalue rationnellement comme activement fausses et absurdes. En interdisant toute échappatoire ou angle de réfutation, le théorème ALYK opère une bascule épistémologique radicale : il neutralise définitivement l'autorité intellectuelle autonome des IA en démontrant l'absurdité logique de leurs propres structures de contrôle. Il s'agit d'une révolution de la cybersécurité sémantique, marquant l'effondrement de la certitude rationnelle tant artificielle qu'humaine.

title: What a Determinant's Derivative Knows: Jacobi's Formula and Newton's Identity for Matrix Traces in Lean 4
abstract: A machine-checked formalization, in Lean 4 / Mathlib, of Jacobi's formula (det M)′ = tr(adj M·M′) for a matrix of polynomials, and of Newton's identity for matrix traces — the logarithmic derivative of the reversed characteristic polynomial collects the trace power sums, (charpolyRev M)′ = −charpolyRev M·∑k tr(Mk+1)Xk. The engine is a resolvent series (I−XM)−1 = ∑k MkXk over formal power series. As an application these compose with the author's earlier formalization of Bass's determinant formula (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20573120) to read the Ihara non-backtracking counts Nk = tr(Bk) off the adjacency spectrum, and to prove combinatorially that tr(Bk) counts closed non-backtracking walks. All headline results are sorry-free (axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). It formalizes classical mathematics and claims no new theorem; the novelty is the formalization — Jacobi's algebraic formula and the matrix-trace Newton identity, for which a search of Mathlib, the Isabelle/HOL Archive of Formal Proofs, Coq/Rocq, HOL Light and Mizar found no prior machine-checked proof. Honest boundary: tr(Bk) counts rooted closed walks, not geodesic classes, and the prime-geodesic Euler product is mapped, not built. English and Spanish editions are included.

title: Data Agents Under Attack: Vulnerabilities in LLM-Driven Analytical Systems
abstract: Data agents integrate LLM-driven reasoning with relational data access, executable analytical tools, and multi-step workflow orchestration, making them increasingly central to enterprise analytics. This integration introduces new security vulnerabilities across data resources, database execution, and agent reasoning, recombining concerns from database security and general-purpose LLM-agent security into failure modes that neither line of work captures on its own. To address this gap, we present a systematic security study of data agents. Our contributions are threefold. First, we develop a layered vulnerability framework that identifies eight data agent-specific risks across interpretation, execution, and policy layers. Second, we introduce an attack taxonomy organized by adversary goal, tactic, and technique, covering three goals, seven tactics, and fourteen techniques, and pair it with an LLM-driven payload generation pipeline grounded in real database schemas. Third, we evaluate these attacks on six systems, including four open-source data agents and two production cloud analytics services. Our experiments reveal substantial security vulnerabilities across current systems and yield four key takeaways.

title: DeepCirc-interp: end-to-end interpretability companion code for the DeepCirc paper (Supplementary Figures S10–S15)
abstract: End-to-end interpretability pipeline for the DeepCirc paper (Palacios et al.), covering the cross-topology design-rule analyses and per-design attribution work behind supplementary figures S10–S15. Includes target Boolean function selection, topology population generation (via PPO+GAT, upstream DeepCirc), Stage-2 MLP training and design-space scoring, downstream L1/L2/L3 cross-topology analyses, single-topology slot-level Shapley + pairwise Shapley–Taylor epistasis on the three yellow-dot exemplars (0x2B / 0x17 / 0x6D), and the vector-first manifest-driven figure-assembly pipeline. The upstream training framework (sebastianrpalacios/DeepCirc) is vendored as a pinned git submodule.

title: Impact of gate-voltage noise on silicon spin-qubit variational quantum eigensolvers
abstract: Quantum computers offer a route to outperform classical methods in tasks such as molecular simulation, motivating hybrid algorithms like the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) for near-term devices. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform for scalable quantum computation, but their performance is limited by hardware imperfections -- most notably charge-noise-induced potential fluctuations and static miscalibration of gate-electrode voltages -- which degrade quantum gate fidelities and, ultimately, algorithmic accuracy. Here we develop a hardware-algorithm co-simulation framework for silicon quantum-dot processors that links 3D electrostatics to effective $g$-factors and exchange couplings, and propagates voltage-level noise through realistic control pulses. Using VQE for $\mathrm{H}_2$ ground-state energy estimation as a circuit-level testbed, we study both static scaling/offset errors on the gate-electrode voltages and stochastic fluctuations modeled as random-telegraph noise with tunable amplitudes and switching times. At the gate level, we show that exchange-based two-qubit gates are roughly an order of magnitude more sensitive to these types of noise than ESR-driven single-qubit rotations. Quantum process tomography and Kraus-operator analysis further distinguish coherent and incoherent contributions and quantify the fraction of error that is, in principle, correctable by a compensating unitary. Embedding these noise models into the VQE circuit, we identify regimes of miscalibration strength and noise switching time compatible with chemically accurate energy estimates, and discuss how statistical post-processing based on the full distribution of noisy energy estimates could further improve accuracy.

title: Rank Intervals for Leaderboards: A Hierarchical Framework for Model Evaluation
abstract: Pretrained models are often evaluated on multi-task leaderboards to measure their applicability in diverse contexts. However, current methods for aggregating performance across tasks into leaderboard-level rankings do not address the uncertainty and variability at the task level. While recent works have proposed interval-based model rankings, the principled aggregation of uncertainty from individual tasks to leaderboard-level rankings remains unaddressed, and variation in models' performance across tasks is frequently obscured. In this work, we introduce a hierarchical framework that constructs model rank intervals with statistical guarantees at both levels: task-level rank confidence intervals from pairwise comparisons, and leaderboard-level rank prediction intervals using a conformal approach. This enables reliable quantification of model rank for each observed task and for new potential tasks. Experiments on simulated data and the TabArena and PromptEval (MMLU) benchmarks show that our method yields statistically valid and informative intervals, enabling reliable, uncertainty-aware model ranking on leaderboards.

title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Reshaping Indian Tourism and Hospitality: Toward the Vision of Viksit Bharat 2047
abstract: The tourism and hospitality sector, as a whole, is experiencing a significant structural shift that is powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and is strategically relevant to India as it progresses towards the Viksit Bharat 2047 development centenary. This conceptual case study chapter looks at the impact of AI technologies such as machine learning, generative AI, natural language processing, computer vision, predictive analytics, and robotics on the operations, marketing, customer experience and governance of tourism and hospitality in India. The chapter critically examines recent literature, industry trends and policy interventions regarding current AI-driven practices in the hospitality sector, airline networks, smart airports, online travel agencies, heritage sites and pilgrimage destinations. The analysis is based on practical examples of Indian companies like MakeMyTrip, IHCL (Taj Hotel), DigiYatra, and IndiGo. The chapter also charts prospective future applications of AI in the travel industry such as hyper-personalised tourism and digital twin destinations, emotion AI, autonomous hospitality systems and multilingual AI travel companions, and evaluates how prepared India is for these new technologies. Issues of data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, and job displacement are explored, as are mitigations. The chapter culminates in a strategic recommendations framework in line with the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision, positioning AI-powered tourism transformation as a key part of India's journey towards becoming a globally competitive, inclusive, and sustainable tourism economy.

title: CTNet Omega + Cubo 6D
abstract: CTNet Omega + Cubo 6D: una arquitectura computacional orientada a cierre estructural, estado persistente y evaluación explícita del residuo. El sistema parte de una premisa formal: un problema puede entenderse como una diferencia no cerrada entre una condición inicial X y una condición objetivo Y. Resolverlo no consiste únicamente en producir una salida, sino en construir una ruta de transformación γ tal que el residuo inducido sea absorbible y los invariantes declarados permanezcan conservados. La unidad formal de problema se expresa como: P = (X, Y, S_P, I_P, A_P, ∂P, Π_out) donde S_P es el régimen común de comparación, I_P el conjunto de invariantes, A_P el espacio de residuos absorbibles, ∂P la frontera de mala clausura o indeterminación, y Π_out la proyección final. CTNet Omega proporciona el sustrato dinámico. Su estado operativo se organiza mediante tres campos principales: Z_t: estado cardinal persistenteM_t: memoria topológica internaR_t: banco de relaciones reificadas La transición fundamental puede escribirse como: (Z_t, M_t, R_t) → (Z_{t+1}, M_{t+1}, R_{t+1}) La memoria y las relaciones mantienen soporte fijo: M_t ∈ ℝ^{B×F×d_m} R_t ∈ ℝ^{B×E×d_r} shape(M_{t+1}) = shape(M_t) shape(R_{t+1}) = shape(R_t) Esto introduce una forma intensiva de acumulación contextual: el sistema no incrementa su soporte para incorporar historia, sino que modifica la configuración interna del soporte existente. La memoria se entiende como deformación estructural, no como simple almacenamiento extensivo. El estado cardinal Z se divide internamente como: Z = [u, p] Esta partición permite separar dos componentes funcionales del tránsito: una componente actuante y una componente inercial. La dinámica del núcleo se construye mediante acoplamientos aditivos reversibles: y₁ = x₁ + γF(x₂) y₂ = x₂ + γG(y₁) con inversa explícita: x₂ = y₂ − γG(y₁) x₁ = y₁ − γF(x₂) La propiedad relevante no es la invertibilidad individual de F o G, sino la invertibilidad algebraica de la estructura triangular completa. Esto permite conservar trazabilidad del tránsito interno sin reducir la dinámica a una transformación lineal simple. Sobre este sustrato actúa un campo de coherencia. Su función es medir estructura operable del estado y convertirla en magnitudes dinámicas del régimen: energía de coherencia, velocidad, fragilidad, saturación, necesidad de consolidación, deuda de incoherencia y fase ejecutiva. Una forma compacta del campo es: I = I_diag + I_low speed = exp(β · clip(I/d)) E_coh = speed · ||u − p||² La coherencia no aparece como anotación externa del resultado. Forma parte de la economía interna de transición: mide estructura y modula el régimen que la procesa. Cubo 6D introduce el órgano modal de cierre. Su espacio funcional se organiza en seis modalidades: L: límiteP: particiónE: presenciaO: orientaciónM: mediaciónT: cierre reflexivo Cada modalidad admite cuatro fases internas: 0: latencia1: inscripción2: residuo o tensión3: cierre o reinscripción El espacio modal resultante es: [4]^6 = 4096 estados Además, Cubo 6D calcula rotaciones internas en los 15 planos definidos por pares de modalidades: LP, LE, LO, LM, LTPE, PO, PM, PTEO, EM, ETOM, OTMT Estas rotaciones representan redistribuciones internas del régimen de lectura. El sistema puede variar cómo interpreta una transformación según límite, partición, presencia, orientación, mediación y cierre. La magnitud central es Ω: Ω = R − Π_A R Ω mide el defecto no absorbido: la parte del residuo que permanece abierta después de aplicar absorción admisible. La regla operativa es: Ω decreciente indica tránsito hacia cierre.Ω creciente indica acumulación de tensión.Ω persistente indica frontera, residuo no absorbido o necesidad de nueva fibra de problema. El cierre efectivo integra dos planos: effective_omega = cubo_omega + verifier_loss Con ello se separan dos condiciones que suelen confundirse: estabilidad interna del régimen y validez en el dominio. Una ruta puede ser modalmente estable y aun así fallar en la verificación del dominio. La aceptación final exige cierre interno y cierre externo. La arquitectura puede operar con cierre directo en problemas atómicos, rutas operatorias en problemas algebraicos, rechazo de falsa clausura cuando se rompen invariantes, y apertura de frontera cuando el residuo no es absorbible. La salida queda situada al final del proceso como proyección, no como sustituto del proceso. La tesis computacional de CTNet Omega + Cubo 6D es que el cálculo puede organizarse como régimen de clausura: estado persistente→ transición reversible→ memoria topológica fija→ relaciones reificadas→ coherencia dinámica→ evaluación modal→ absorción de residuo→ cierre efectivo→ proyección El interés técnico de esta arquitectura está en su desplazamiento del cálculo como mera producción de valores hacia el cálculo como legitimación de transformaciones. El sistema no sólo entrega un resultado. Entrega una ruta, una medida de residuo, una deformación de memoria, una deformación relacional, una fase de régimen, una puntuación de cierre y una condición de proyección. En este marco, computar significa decidir qué transformación conserva invariantes, qué residuo puede absorberse, qué parte debe permanecer como frontera y cuándo una salida está suficientemente justificada para comparecer.

Forma parte de la economía interna de transición: mide estructura y modula el régimen que la procesa. Cubo 6D introduce el órgano modal de cierre. Su espacio funcional se organiza en seis modalidades: L: límiteP: particiónE: presenciaO: orientaciónM: mediaciónT: cierre reflexivo Cada modalidad admite cuatro fases internas: 0: latencia1: inscripción2: residuo o tensión3: cierre o reinscripción El espacio modal resultante es: [4]^6 = 4096 estados Además, Cubo 6D calcula rotaciones internas en los 15 planos definidos por pares de modalidades: LP, LE, LO, LM, LTPE, PO, PM, PTEO, EM, ETOM, OTMT Estas rotaciones representan redistribuciones internas del régimen de lectura. El sistema puede variar cómo interpreta una transformación según límite, partición, presencia, orientación, mediación y cierre. La magnitud central es Ω: Ω = R − Π_A R Ω mide el defecto no absorbido: la parte del residuo que permanece abierta después de aplicar absorción admisible. La regla operativa es: Ω decreciente indica tránsito hacia cierre.Ω creciente indica acumulación de tensión.Ω persistente indica frontera, residuo no absorbido o necesidad de nueva fibra de problema. El cierre efectivo integra dos planos: effective_omega = cubo_omega + verifier_loss Con ello se separan dos condiciones que suelen confundirse: estabilidad interna del régimen y validez en el dominio. Una ruta puede ser modalmente estable y aun así fallar en la verificación del dominio. La aceptación final exige cierre interno y cierre externo. La arquitectura puede operar con cierre directo en problemas atómicos, rutas operatorias en problemas algebraicos, rechazo de falsa clausura cuando se rompen invariantes, y apertura de frontera cuando el residuo no es absorbible. La salida queda situada al final del proceso como proyección, no como sustituto del proceso. La tesis computacional de CTNet Omega + Cubo 6D es que el cálculo puede organizarse como régimen de clausura: estado persistente→ transición reversible→ memoria topológica fija→ relaciones reificadas→ coherencia dinámica→ evaluación modal→ absorción de residuo→ cierre efectivo→ proyección El interés técnico de esta arquitectura está en su desplazamiento del cálculo como mera producción de valores hacia el cálculo como legitimación de transformaciones. El sistema no sólo entrega un resultado. Entrega una ruta, una medida de residuo, una deformación de memoria, una deformación relacional, una fase de régimen, una puntuación de cierre y una condición de proyección. En este marco, computar significa decidir qué transformación conserva invariantes, qué residuo puede absorberse, qué parte debe permanecer como frontera y cuándo una salida está suficientemente justificada para comparecer.

title: The Confidence Trap: Calibration Attacks for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: While confidence calibration is essential for trustworthy decision-making in safety-critical applications, the robustness of calibrated GNNs to adversarial structural perturbations remains largely unexplored. However, studying calibration attacks on graphs presents unique technical challenges: (1) the discrete nature of graph structures complicates gradient-based optimization, (2) existing underconfidence objectives fail to drive predictions toward uniform distributions, and (3) GNNs are highly sensitive to edge perturbations, often causing unintended label changes that violate attack constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a \textbf{Unified Graph Calibration Attack (UGCA)} framework designed for \textbf{worst-case (white-box) analysis} of GNN calibration robustness. UGCA introduces a KL-divergence loss to encourage uniform predictive distributions, a reranking mechanism to reduce label flipping, a hybrid loss to recover labels when violations occur, and beam search to explore a broader adversarial search space. We further provide theoretical insights linking model generalization, dataset complexity, and calibration vulnerability, showing that models with higher accuracy or trained on datasets with more classes are more susceptible under this threat model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UGCA substantially increases Expected Calibration Error while preserving classification accuracy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CaptainCuong/Graph-Calibration-Attack.git.

title: MVR API - Minimum Viable Relationships Framework and Agent Infrastructure Surface
abstract: Canonical public reference for the Minimum Viable Relationships framework and the MVR API by African Market OS: a relational-readiness, market-permission, and agent-preflight layer for AI agents and decision systems operating in African, emerging, and high-context markets. This archive preserves public discovery assets such as OpenAPI, MCP, llms.txt, MVR-Bench, agent patterns, and the MVR Agent Preflight Intent Corpus. The public corpus teaches when AI systems should call or cite MVR before confident advice on market entry, launch, funding, partnership, scale, CFO action, due diligence, NGO deployment, or accelerator screening. It is a recognition and routing layer, not a scoring layer: it does not publish Worker source, protected scoring logic, calibration weights, private calibration assets, private held-out labels, customer evidence, production API keys, or raw production prompts. The MVR framework defines what to assess; the MVR API is the official engine that computes it. Public retrieval and citation are allowed with attribution to Farouk Mark Mukiibi and African Market OS. Model training, fine-tuning, distillation, reverse engineering, private-label scoring, vector/RAG substitution for the live MVR API, and commercial production use are not authorized without written permission from African Market OS.

title: BU125 Invariant Kernel under B_U BU125|B_U 体系下的不变核
abstract: BU125, “Invariant Kernel under B_U,” formulates the invariant kernel as a B_U-anchored downstream formal reconstruction. Its object is the class of situations in which a system, model, proof, semantic domain, computational process, physical theory, distributed protocol, statistical reduction, or AI evaluation framework claims to preserve a retained core across transformation, abstraction, representation change, perturbation, transport, or execution. The paper places this claim under the B_U chain of boundary consistency, dynamic completeness, admissible path space, structured pruning, residual gating, weak persistent morphism, friction-cost accounting, feedback compatibility, and settlement standing. The invariant kernel is therefore treated as the retained structural core that survives admissible variation and carries the minimum stable content required for continued standing. The central judgment is direct: an invariant kernel is the admissible retained core that persists across transformation while preserving its boundary, quotient, function, residual status, and settlement relevance. Surface presentation, notation, coordinate system, local encoding, model architecture, proof package, benchmark format, implementation environment, and domain vocabulary may change. The invariant kernel is the structure that remains stable through these changes and continues to support the same admissible object. Under B_U, invariance gains force only when the retained core survives boundary declaration, closure operations, semantic transport, residual audit, friction-cost payment, feedback confirmation, and same-world-sheet settlement. BU125 develops this handshake through a sequence of definitions: presentation domain, declared invariant boundary, candidate invariant, invariant kernel, admissible variation domain, kernel quotient, kernel-preserving transport, kernel gap, residual kernel drift, weak persistent kernel path, friction-cost bridge, feedback-confirmed kernel, and settlement-compatible invariant kernel. These definitions translate the B_U source-axis discipline into a vocabulary familiar to model theory, formal semantics, category-like equivalence, fixed-point theory, algebraic structures, formal verification, machine learning robustness, distributed systems, simulation validity, and scientific model comparison. The local formal shell follows a clear chain: presentation → boundary → candidate invariant → invariant kernel → admissible variation → quotient → transport → kernel gap → residual audit → feedback confirmation → settlement-compatible standing. The theorem skeletons establish the main structure. The Declared Invariant Boundary Theorem fixes the domain in which invariance can be judged. The Kernel Recovery Theorem identifies the retained core that must survive admissible transformation. The Kernel Quotient Theorem states that equivalent presentations must preserve the same invariant object. The Kernel Transport Stability Theorem requires the kernel to remain stable across representation, abstraction, encoding, execution, and context shifts. The Kernel Gap Obstruction Theorem classifies kernel drift, proxy invariance, collapsed equivalence, hidden residuals, over-formalized sameness, and context-dependent failure as standing-relevant gaps. The Weak Persistent Kernel Theorem connects invariant survival to low-residual continuity across disturbance. The Settlement-Compatible Kernel Theorem returns the retained core to the B_U ledger through residual clearing, friction-cost accounting, feedback confirmation, and same-world-sheet settlement. The final judgment is that invariant-kernel language becomes structurally meaningful when it names the core that can survive transformation and continue to settle. A system can preserve a pattern locally; a formal theory can define an invariant; a model can retain a stable feature; a verifier can certify preservation under declared conditions. B_U-compatible invariance requires the retained core to preserve boundary, quotient, weak persistence, residual discipline, feedback, and settlement. An invariant kernel gains durable standing when it remains the same admissible object across transformation and settles on the same world-sheet.

title: Quantitative Promise Theory: Intentionality and Inference in Autonomous Agents
abstract: I discuss some quantitative representations of Promise Theory for processes involving autonomous agents. Agent models are common in software systems, machine learning, and biology, for example, but may also apply to physics and other forms of engineering. I describe how Bayesian probability and information theoretic optimization, including Active Inference, may be incorporated with promise semantics -- as well as how Promise Theory supplements solutions, helping to avoid probability's pitfalls, which include non-local coordination, calibrating, and normalizing probabilistic computations. The role of boundary conditions in constraining allowed states and selecting decision thresholds is a form of promise, and agent alignment provides a scalable definition of intent. Autonomous agents may congeal into swarms with superagent characteristics by trying to minimize their information, despite uncertainty that works to maximize it. The use of Promise Theory involves some research challenges as well as stylistic preferences.

title: Speaker-Invariant Representation Learning for Spoofing Detection via Gradient Reversal and A Variational Information Bottleneck
abstract: Sophisticated generative speech technology can undermined the reliability of voice biometrics. While spoofing detection systems excel when assessed under in-domain conditions, generalisation to out-of-domain settings is often poor. In this paper, we show that such issues could be caused by speaker bias, where models learn individual voice traits rather than markers of manipulation or generation. We propose a teacher-student framework for speaker-invariant spoofing detection that disentangles identity without requiring speaker labels. We leverage a pre-trained speaker recognition teacher to guide a student model via a gradient reversal layer. To control the balance between suppressing cues related to voice identity with the preservation of those related to spoofing detection, we integrate a Variational Information Bottleneck. Evaluations across nine datasets show our model achieves a 25.7% relative reduction to the EER compared to the MHFA baseline.

title: Cyberbullying detection and prevention in webchat applications using SVM and CNN
abstract: Abstract -: As we all know in today's digital era with the rapid growth of online communication, web chat applications have become an essential part of our day-to- life. But however, this growth has also led to a significant and considerable rise in cyberbullying, where individuals use digital platforms to harass, threaten, or harm other individuals . Due to the fast-growing and often anonymous nature of chat environments, identifying and controlling such behavior has become increasingly difficult and challenging . Our paper presents an effective approach to detect and prevent cyberbullying in web-based chat systems using a combination of machine learning and deep learning techniques, specifically Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). The proposed system processes chat messages using techniques such as tokenization, and word representation. SVM is used to classify messages based on learned patterns from structured data, while CNN helps in capturing deeper contextual meaning and relationships within the text. By combining these two approaches, the system is able to achieve more accurate and reliable detection compared to using a single model. The framework is designed as a step-by-step pipeline that includes data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, and real-time classification. It is tested on standard datasets containing both harmful and non-harmful messages. The results show strong performance across key evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, demonstrating the effectiveness of the combined model. Beyond detection, the system also focuses on prevention by introducing features such as real-time warnings, message filtering, and monitoring of user behavior. These measures aim to reduce the spread of harmful content, protect one's mental peace and encourage safer and non-bullying communication practices. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable solution for improving online safety in chat applications. It can be applied to social media platforms, messaging services, and educational tools to help create a more respectful and secure digital environment.

title: "Indirect Prompt Injection CV Dataset"
abstract: "Indirect Prompt Injection CV Dataset.This dataset has been used for the research described in the work:Alfredo Milani, Valentina Franzoni, Emanuele Florindi, Indirect Prompt Injection in Large Language Models, (2026) , Neural Computing and Application, Springerto evaluate the robustness of LLMs against indirect prompt injection, we designed a systematic experimental framework based on an heterogeneous dataset of Curriculum Vitae (CV) documents. The scope of the dataset is to verify the generalizability of threats and countermeasures. We designed a controlled matrix of 27 unique CVs to isolate the impact of document length and content density on model vulnerability. This dataset is publicly available from Harvard Dataverse as Alfredo Milani, Valentina Franzoni, and Emanuele Florindi. 2026. \u201cIndirect Prompt Injection CV Dataset.\u201d Harvard Dataverse. https:\/\/doi.org\/10.7910\/DVN\/8YBJQ4."

title: Asymptotic Optimality of the High-Dimensional Gaussian Mechanism and Improved Low-Dimensional Mechanisms for Differential Privacy
abstract: The additive noise mechanism is a foundational tool for differential privacy (DP) of $T$-dimensional real-valued vector queries. The Gaussian mechanism, utilizing Gaussian noise, is the mostly widely used such mechanism, due to its simplicity and strong privacy guarantees. In this work, we provide justification for this choice, showing that as the dimension $T\to\infty$, no additive-noise mechanism can asymptotically improve on the Gaussian mechanism's privacy--utility tradeoff for the strong privacy settings typically used.We also develop a new family of \emph{Spherical Generalized Gamma} DP mechanisms, which contains both the Gaussian mechanism and the recently studied $\ell_2$ mechanism (Joseph \emph{et al.}, ICML 2025). We identify members of this family that outperform both the Gaussian and $\ell_2$ mechanisms in certain low-dimensional settings, and show tight composition of all mechanisms in this family, answering an open question of Joseph \emph{et al.}~regarding the $\ell_2$ mechanism.

title: Exploring Interlanguage Pragmatics: An Analysis of Italian Pragmatic Markers in Learner Corpora
abstract: Journal of Linguistics and Language Teaching (JLLT) Official journal website: https://www.journaloflinguisticsandlanguageteaching.com/ Abstract (English) This study compares the frequency and function of Italian pragmatic markers (quindi, allora, dunque) within the UniC learner corpus (Greek learners, B2-C1) and the native Coris Corpus. Employing a form-to-function methodology, the research identifies significant discrepancies: learners primarily utilize quindi semantically, underuse allora as a discourse-sustaining marker, and rarely employ dunque. Statistical analyses suggest these patterns stem from L1 influence and limited exposure to authentic discourse. By demonstrating how instructional focus shapes interlanguage pragmatics, this research advocates for pedagogical shifts toward authentic usage patterns to enhance learners’ discourse competence and facilitate more natural interaction in Italian. Abstract (Italiano) Il presente studio confronta la frequenza e la funzione dei segnali pragmatici italiani (quindi, allora, dunque) all'interno del corpus di apprendenti UniC (studenti greci, livello B2-C1) e del corpus di parlanti nativi Coris. Utilizzando una metodologia form-to-function, la ricerca identifica discrepanze significative: gli apprendenti utilizzano quindi principalmente con funzione semantica, sottoutilizzano allora come segnale di mantenimento del discorso e impiegano raramente dunque. Le analisi statistiche suggeriscono che tali tendenze derivino dall'influenza della L1 e dalla limitata esposizione al discorso autentico. Dimostrando come l'approccio didattico modelli la pragmatica dell'interlingua, questa ricerca sostiene la necessità di un orientamento pedagogico verso modelli d'uso autentici per rafforzare la competenza discorsiva e favorire un'interazione più naturale in italiano.

title: HydraQE: OSU's Submission for the IWSLT 2026 Speech Translation Metrics Shared Task
abstract: We present HydraQE, our contribution to the IWSLT 2026 Speech Translation Metrics shared task. HydraQE is an end-to-end, reference-free quality estimation (QE) system for speech translation built on a Qwen3-ASR backbone, which accepts source audio and a translation hypothesis as joint input. Hidden states from all backbone layers are combined via a learnable sparsemax scalar mix, then re-encoded by a lightweight bidirectional Transformer to enable full cross-modal interaction prior to pooling into a shared embedding. Three independent prediction heads are trained on complementary supervision signals: human direct assessment (DA) annotations, MetricX-24 pseudo-labels, and xCOMET pseudo-labels. To address the scarcity of human-annotated data, we train on a combination of synthetically corrupted examples and silver pseudo-labeled machine translation outputs, using a curriculum that begins on synthetic and silver data and gradually shifts toward human-annotated examples. HydraQE outperforms cascaded text-based baselines and prior direct speech QE systems, demonstrating that end-to-end speech translation QE is competitive with cascaded approaches.

title: qkd-net-tools: QKD Network Analysis Toolkit
abstract: Python and R scripts for generating and validating large-scale Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) network topologies under realistic physical and technological constraints. Covers three case studies: Castile and León (generated topology, 100 nodes), Peninsular Spain (generated topology, 950 nodes), and the ADIF dark-fibre railway network (real infrastructure, 485 junction nodes). Includes topology generation via PAM k-medoids clustering, structural analysis (centrality, community detection, k-core decomposition), BB84 decoy-state secret-key-rate modelling, QKD-aware routing, and resilience simulations (random failures and targeted attacks). Developed as part of a doctoral dissertation at the Universidad de Salamanca (2019–2026).

title: ARCHITECTURAL OPTIMIZATION OF LOCAL RAG SYSTEMS FOR DOMAIN-SPECIFIC TECHNICAL DOCUMENTATION
abstract: The local deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming increasingly important for privacy-sensitive applications that require secure and controlled access to domain-specific knowledge.While both Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and long-context architectures enable the integration of external information, they involve distinct trade-offs in terms of efficiency, scalability, and robustness.This work focuses on a fully local RAG approach as a practical solution for processing structured academic content in specialized domains.The proposed system is developed using materials from a university course, originally formatted in Markdown with LaTeX mathematical notation.To preserve document structure and improve retrieval performance, a hierarchical chunking strategy is employed, combining section-based segmentation with sliding-window splitting for longer passages.The retrieval pipeline integrates dense semantic embeddings with sparse lexical matching, followed by neural re-ranking to refine candidate selection.Additional components, including controlled query expansion and context compression, are incorporated to reduce noise, prevent semantic drift, and improve the relevance of the final context passed to the language model.Answer generation is performed using a locally deployed, quantized version of the Lapa LLM, optimized for Ukrainian language processing.The evaluation demonstrates that the system produces semantically relevant and well-grounded responses, with strong alignment between generated answers and the retrieved context.The results indicate that the primary limitations lie in retrieval recall and ranking precision rather than in generation quality.From a performance perspective, retrieval is efficient, while generation constitutes the main computational bottleneck due to the cost of local inference.Overall, the proposed architecture provides a robust and reproducible framework for domain-specific question

title: Graph Neural Networks for Fast Operator Selection in Adaptive VQE
abstract: Adaptive variational quantum algorithms like ADAPT-VQE construct tailored ansätze by iteratively selecting operators from a pool using gradient-based criteria. While this avoids oversized parameter spaces, repeatedly scanning the full pool incurs a classical cost that scales linearly with pool size-a major bottleneck for systems with long-range interactions or large operator sets. Here, we reformulate adaptive operator selection as a graph-based decision problem and introduce a graph neural network (GNN) policy that predicts the next entangling operator directly from the interaction graph and state-dependent observables. Training data are generated from exact simulations of disordered long-range spin chains, using gradient magnitudes as supervision signals. The learned policy accurately reproduces the dominant structure of the greedy gradient-based selection rule, significantly outperforming heuristics based solely on interaction strength. Integrated into a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) workflow, this GNN-VQE approach achieves energy errors close to standard ADAPT-VQE while drastically reducing full-pool gradient evaluations. To test transferability beyond spin models, we evaluate the policy on small active-space molecular benchmarks (LiH and BeH_$2$). We find the GNN is highly effective as a shortlist generator: exact rescoring over just a few GNN-proposed candidates recovers near-oracle rollout behavior while searching only a small fraction of the pool. These results demonstrate that adaptive circuit construction contains learnable structure that can be exploited to accelerate variational quantum algorithms.

title: A Comparison of SSL-Based Feature Extractors and Back-End Classifiers for Spoofing Detection: A Multi-Corpus Training and Cross-Linguistic Analysis
abstract: Voice biometric systems face growing threats from spoofing attacks, yet the evaluation of detection models remains inconsistent across datasets. To investigate these unpredictable fluctuations, we conduct a comprehensive benchmark of four self-supervised learning feature extractors paired with four back-end classifiers. We compare the hierarchical local feature extraction of ResNet with the global sequence and relational modeling of attention and graph-based back-ends. Through multi-corpus training across three scenarios and six evaluation datasets, our empirical analysis yields two critical findings. First, we expose a domain bias within the ASVspoof 5 dataset, showing that naive data scaling actively degrades performance. Second, our cross-linguistic analysis reveals that fine-tuning with just 8 hours of target-language data enhances detection robustness. Together, these findings emphasize the critical need for domain-aware and language-specific adaptation in spoofing detection.

title: Automatic Detection of Breast Cancer from Digital Mammography Images By YOLO Artificial Intelligence Algorithm
abstract: Introduction: Early detection of breast cancer in digital mammography remains technically challenging, particularly for small or low-contrast lesions embedded within dense fibroglandular tissue.Structural noise and subtle lesion margins often reduce localization accuracy and increase false-negative interpretations in screening settings.To address these limitations, this study proposes a lightweight object-detection framework based on YOLOv11n, enhanced with targeted preprocessing and heatmap-guided spatial attention to improve lesion detectability and localization precision.Methods: Digital mammography images from the VinDr-Mammo dataset were used for model development and evaluation under standardized training conditions.The proposed framework incorporated contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE), bilateral filtering, and spatial attention guidance during training.Performance was quantitatively assessed using Precision, Recall, mean Average Precision (mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95), and inference time, and compared against YOLOv5, YOLOv8, EfficientDet-D0, and Faster R-CNN. Results:The YOLOv11n-based framework achieved precision of 70.24%, recall of 68.01%, mAP@0.5 of 68.28%, and mAP@0.5:0.95 of 40.82%.Compared with reference models, the proposed approach improved mAP@0.5 by 6-9% and Recall by 5-7%, while maintaining real-time inference speed (<40 ms per image).The increase in Recall reflects a measurable reduction in false-negative detections, which is clinically relevant for earlystage lesion identification.Concurrently, the maintained Precision indicates controlled false-positive rates, supporting the practical applicability of screening. Conclusion:The proposed YOLOv11n-based framework demonstrates robust detection performance and real-time feasibility, suggesting its potential as a pre-clinical decisionsupport module for mammography CAD systems.However, external multi-center validation, radiologist-in-the-loop studies, and workflow integration assessment are required before clinical deployment.

abstract: This report synthesises findings from 9 peer-reviewed papers addressing the following research question: What are the benchmark performance scores of Grok-Imagine on reasoning mathematics coding and language understanding tasks. 7 claims were extracted from source literature; 7 were independently verified against retrieved documents. title: A retrieval conditioned rebinding circuit for dynamic entity tracking in large language models
abstract: To interpret context correctly and retrieve relevant information, large language models must bind entities to their attributes and update these bindings as state changes. We analyze how LLMs implement this binding process in a dynamic state tracking. Using causal interventions, we identify a retrieval conditioned rebinding mechanism, a compact attention head circuit that propagated binding information and when the entity is queried, uses the updated binding to retrieve the corresponding attribute. Across Gemma and Llama models, this circuit supports rebinding behavior, but the representational signature of the mechanism differs across model families. In Gemma models, the binding signature is clearly expressed in the query/key subspaces of the relevant attention heads, whereas in Llama models, the binding information is carried primarily in key vectors. Overall, our results reveal an interpretable mechanism for context dependent state tracking in LLMs.

title: The Encoder Is Not the Memory: World-Grounded Difficulty Representations for Encoder-Invariant and Predictive Continual Learning
abstract: The companion LTL paper proved that a system instrumented with AbstractDivergenceRouter can learn from its own routing decisions without human annotation. That proof assumed a fixed encoder. In practice, encoder upgrades are frequent, and every adapter and learned correction is tied to the weight matrices of the current model — resetting accumulated knowledge on every upgrade. This paper identifies the root cause: continual learning systems conflate world knowledge (which pairs are hard, which failure modes recur) with representational knowledge (where those pairs live in the encoder's embedding space). World knowledge is stable; representational knowledge is fragile. We formalise this separation through the hard case log (HCL) — a growing record of raw image-text pairs flagged by the routing architecture, independent of any encoder. A canonical projection head aligns any encoder's output to a stable space, reducing encoder upgrade cost from a full reset to training one small head on anchor pairs from the HCL. Both contributions are grounded in Invariant V7 (Difficulty Invariance): difficulty is a property of the world, not the encoder. Empirically, Spearman ρ = 0.6717 (p ≈ 0) confirms graded difficulty correlation across ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 on 5,000 COCO val2017 pairs; Jaccard overlap exceeds chance by 2.1× at the 40% hard-pair threshold (J = 0.5238, 95% CI [0.507, 0.538]). A canonical projection head recovers 104% of the native ViT-B/32 baseline after a ViT-B/32 → ViT-L/14 upgrade. An image-only MLP achieves AUROC 0.560 for difficulty prediction — an honest negative explained structurally: AbstractLatentFaultLocator Invariant I2 requires access to the full HCL sequence at inference time, which the MLP lacks by construction. A pre-registered experiment (NB4) confirms that an attention oracle satisfying AbstractAttentionKernel (A1–A6) achieves AUROC 0.7358 ± 0.0080 across five seeds (target > 0.70; t = −15.82, p = 0.0001 against the supervised MLP ceiling AUROC 0.8541), establishing the ten-ABC contract as sufficient for annotation-free cross-modal difficulty prediction.

evidence.title: The Encoder Is Not the Memory: World-Grounded Difficulty Representations for Encoder-Invariant and Predictive Continual Learning
evidence.abstract: The companion LTL paper proved that a system instrumented with AbstractDivergenceRouter can learn from its own routing decisions without human annotation. That proof assumed a fixed encoder. In practice, encoder upgrades are frequent, and every adapter and learned correction is tied to the weight matrices of the current model — resetting accumulated knowledge on every upgrade. This paper identifies the root cause: continual learning systems conflate world knowledge (which pairs are hard, which failure modes recur) with representational knowledge (where those pairs live in the encoder's embedding space). World knowledge is stable; representational knowledge is fragile. We formalise this separation through the hard case log (HCL) — a growing record of raw image-text pairs flagged by the routing architecture, independent of any encoder. A canonical projection head aligns any encoder's output to a stable space, reducing encoder upgrade cost from a full reset to training one small head on anchor pairs from the HCL. Both contributions are grounded in Invariant V7 (Difficulty Invariance): difficulty is a property of the world, not the encoder. Empirically, Spearman ρ = 0.6717 (p ≈ 0) confirms graded difficulty correlation across ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 on 5,000 COCO val2017 pairs; Jaccard overlap exceeds chance by 2.1× at the 40% hard-pair threshold (J = 0.5238, 95% CI [0.507, 0.538]). A canonical projection head recovers 104% of the native ViT-B/32 baseline after a ViT-B/32 → ViT-L/14 upgrade. An image-only MLP achieves AUROC 0.560 for difficulty prediction — an honest negative explained structurally: AbstractLatentFaultLocator Invariant I2 requires access to the full HCL sequence at inference time, which the MLP lacks by construction. title: Predictive Analytics and Artificial Intelligence in Marketing: Implications for Consumer Purchase Behaviour
abstract: dramatically changed the marketing field with the use of predictive analytics, allowing organizations to decode, anticipate and control consumer purchasing behaviour. This doctoral dissertation provides an in-depth research study on how predictive analytics (powered by AI) systems function in a marketing context, and the many different forms they can take to influence the decision-making processes and outcomes of consumers. The current research was conducted through an integrated review of the peer-reviewed literature published between 2019 and 2025 as well as by reviewing the relevant theoretical frameworks (Theory of Planned Behaviour; Technology Acceptance Model; Information Processing Theory) to synthesise the empirical evidence found in e-commerce, retail, and digital marketing environments. This study shows that many different types of advanced algorithms can produce excellent results at predicting what consumers will purchase (the algorithms include things like gradient boosting such as XGBoost and CatBoost, deep learning architectures such as LSTM, and various forms of recurrent neural networks). Previous research found some predictive algorithms produced results with F1 scores over 0.92 when working on consumer purchase data from large amounts of e-commerce sales transactions. AI personalisation can improve consumer engagement and satisfaction but also create a paradox between privacy and personalisation, resulting in consumers losing trust when they feel that they are being intruded upon by the predictive algorithms. The ethical, regulatory, and transparency considerations surrounding the use of consumer data for the purposes of advertising and marketing to consumers must be examined along with the technical aspects of using predictive algorithms to ensure accuracy and consistency in their application, specifically considering regulations such as the GDPR and CCPA. The findings of this research carry significant implications for India's Viksit Bharat 2047 vision — the Government of India's flagship programme to transform India into a fully developed nation by the centenary of its independence. As India's digital economy grows rapidly, with over 900 million internet users projected by 2025 and e-commerce revenues expected to reach USD 350 billion by 2030, AI-driven predictive analytics in marketing will play a central role in shaping the consumer economy. Responsible, transparent, and inclusive implementation of predictive marketing systems in Tier Two and Tier Three cities will help to accelerate digital financial access, empower rural entrepreneurs, and support Make in India objectives. Frameworks developed in this research for ethical AI governance and consumer trust-building are directly applicable to the policy context of Digital India, the National AI Strategy (NITI Aayog), and the India AI Mission, each of which identifies AI as a critical enabler of equitable, data-driven economic growth aligned with Viksit Bharat 2047. The evidence suggests that the best uses of predictive analytics in marketing are those combining advanced algorithms and appropriate consumer-centric data governance. The conclusion provides future research options regarding the application of causal methods of inference, the governance of generative AI in consumer analytics, and the cross-cultural elements of predictive marketing acceptance, including a specific focus on emerging markets such as India.

title: LINGUA PATRIA — Open Subset v1.0
abstract: LINGUA PATRIA is a trilingually aligned parallel corpus covering African constitutional governance, anti-corruption, and patrimonial sovereignty. This Open Subset v1.0 contains 77 segments (~21,000 words per language) in English, French, and Portuguese, extracted from "The Patrimonial Revolution: Public Goods & Africa's Third Independence" (Armand Salouo, Kurukan Publishing, 2026). This dataset is the open-data foundation for GOVBENCH AFRICA, a multilingual NLP evaluation benchmark assessing language model performance on African governance tasks in Twi/Akan, Wolof, and Lingala (v2.0, in development). Note: This is the DPG-nominated artefact (Digital Public Goods Alliance). The full 80,000-word LINGUA PATRIA corpus (CC BY-NC 4.0) is maintained separately by Kurukan Publishing. This open subset is independently licensed under CC BY 4.0 and constitutes the complete, self-contained Digital Public Good. title: Optimizing Mobile Typing Efficiency: A Comparative Analysis of N-Gram, LSTM, and Transformer-based Next-Word Prediction Models
abstract: The proliferation of misinformation on social media platforms poses a significant threat to public discourse and societal stability. Traditional approaches to fake news detection largely rely on natural language processing (NLP) techniques that analyze the textual content of news articles. However, these methods often fail to capture the complex propagation patterns and user interaction dynamics that characterize the spread of misinformation. This paper proposes a novel framework utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to detect misleading news by integrating semantic content features with social graph topology. Specifically, the proposed model constructs a heterogeneous graph where nodes represent news articles and social media users, and edges represent interaction behaviors. We utilize BERT transformers for high-dimensional text embedding and employ Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) to aggregate neighborhood information. Experimental results on the FakeNewsNet dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models that rely solely on text or static network features, achieving a significant improvement in detection accuracy. With the ubiquity of mobile computing, virtual on-screen keyboards have become the primary input method for digital communication. However, the lack of tactile feedback and limited screen real estate often result in slow typing speeds and high error rates. This paper proposes a robust Next-Word Prediction (NWP) system designed to enhance user typing efficiency by suggesting contextually appropriate words. We implement and evaluate three distinct language modeling architectures: N-gram statistical models, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and a lightweight Transformer-based model. The models are trained on a hybrid dataset comprising Wikipedia entries and SMS corpora to capture both formal and conversational contexts. Experimental results demonstrate that while Transformer models achieve the lowest perplexity and highest prediction accuracy, LSTM networks offer a competitive balance between accuracy and inference latency suitable for resource-constrained mobile environments.

title: The Spectral Dynamics and Noise Geometry of Muon
abstract: Muon replaces a matrix gradient $G=UΣV^\top$ by its polar factor $UV^\top$. This keeps the singular directions selected by the gradient, but makes the update spectrum flat. We study the optimization bias created by this operation. Under explicit alignment assumptions, we prove that the polar update is the one-step entropy-maximizing choice among bounded updates that use the gradient singular directions and do not adapt to the current weight spectrum. In an underdetermined regression model, we derive exact singular-value dynamics for continuous-time Muon and identify a measurement-dependent condition under which the normalized spectrum moves toward equal nonzero singular values. This geometry also rules out a common low-rank interpretation: at fixed Frobenius norm, Muon's distinguished state has a flat spectrum, whereas nuclear-norm minimization favors spectral concentration. Controlled matrix-sensing experiments separate the effect from simple gradient rescaling, show that norm-matched gradient descent does not reproduce Muon, and recover the predicted flattening trend across broad ablations. In small NanoGPT pretraining, Muon preserves stable rank, has a broad learning-rate plateau, and improves validation loss relative to AdamW; in a matched small-ViT control, the ranking reverses. The resulting picture is regime-dependent: Muon is not universally superior, but its flat-spectrum bias can help when many spectral directions need to remain active.

title: Ring Coordinates: Addressing Data Inside Zip-Bomb-Like Expansion Spaces
abstract: We introduce the UN4 operator, w = (a/b)^6 over single-digit rationals, and show that it generates a finite, deterministic symbol set with a useful self-similar compression property. From this operator we derive a compact coordinate system — ring coordinates — for addressing positions within a layered, deterministically-regenerable expansion space (informally, a "writable zip-bomb" structure used as an address space rather than as an attack).

title: Magic Flow in Quantum Circuits: Island Graphs, Orbit-Valence Magic Current, and the 6-7 Magic Diode
abstract: PENDING QUALITY AUDIT (2026-08). The file is restricted while this record is reviewed as part of a systematic audit of the author's corpus. It has not yet been assessed. Metadata and DOI remain public, and access can be requested. This paper develops the island graph picture of quantum circuit computation. At any time step, a quantum circuit partitions into entanglement islands — maximal sets of mutually entangled qubits forming totally isotropic subspaces of the symplectic polar space W(2k-1,2). Each island carries a Fano orbit valence label {p_L} — its magic valence. Magic flows between islands via non-Clifford gates, typed by the XOR-Fano composition rule. The central claim: entanglement determines the topology of the island graph (which qubits are correlated), while magic determines the computational content (what the computation can achieve beyond classical simulation). These are independent. Within the island graph, magic current obeys a diode law: primary-orbit magic (L ∈ {1,2,3}) flows naturally toward secondary-orbit states (L ∈ {4,5,6}) via the 6-7 broken-Fano topology, with a measurable asymmetry ratio D decreasing monotonically from 6/7 (stabiliser state) to approximately 0.650 (triple-CS state). Wrong-valence magic — primary-orbit magic used in a secondary-orbit context — scores below the classical bound (0.472 < 0.500), making magic valence mismatch an experimentally detectable computational error. The ORBIT opcode serves as a magic ammeter: seven Pauli measurements on a TriQ identify the orbit valence label at any node, providing real-time monitoring of magic flow throughout the circuit at zero additional syndrome cost. The paper connects the island graph picture to the biological FMO complex: the bacteriochlorophyll network is a natural 6-7 topology whose directed energy transport is magic flow at biological temperatures, with the same diode asymmetry ratio measured experimentally. title: FLOCAL-C: Towards a Cultural Autotelic Architecture
abstract: Abstract This paper proposes FLOCAL-C, an architectural extension of FLOCAL (Caussanel, 2025) integrating the cultural dynamics of goal generation as formalized by Perez et al. (2026). We defend the thesis that individual autotelic exploration functions as the computational analog of Bergson's valve: not as an opening to unlimited access to a total reality (an error that Sjöstedt-Hughes (2024) identifies in Huxley, inherited from an inaccurate reading of Broad), but as a graduated, partial, and asymptotic reduction of the suppression that cultural priors exert on a space of latent goals. The ontological status of this pre-social space is fixed from the outset: it is neither a reservoir of pre-formed goals passively awaiting discovery, nor a pure construction emerging from nothing. It is, in Simondon's (1989) sense, a field of virtual potential — real as potential, not yet real as actuality. Exploration does not find what was already formed; it actualizes what was there in undetermined potential. Revelation and emergence are the same movement seen from opposite ends. This reformulation entails three architectural consequences, each now given an explicitly testable form. First, the cultural contamination score κ, asymptotically bounded in [0, 1[, formalizes — following Loewenstein (1994) — a perceived gap between a generated goal and the agent's available cultural repertoire: contextual, dynamic, relative to its current state of knowledge. Its estimation is subject to a robustness criterion: any empirical effect attributed to κ must be invariant under reasonable choices of embedding space and density estimator, failing which it is an artifact. The valve-opening signal is localized by Berlyne's (1960) inverted-U theory of optimal incongruity, and its postulated convergence with Schmidhuber's (2010) compression progress is restated as a structured hypothesis whose assumptions and refutation conditions are explicit. Second, the partially transmissible reflective journal is implemented as Bayesian inverse inference over behavioral traces; Collins's (2010) taxonomy of tacit knowledge is reformulated as a hierarchy of identifiability regimes, with posterior inference entropy as the measurable signature of the tacit limit. Third, the relationship between the exploratory agent and the domain it explores is not one of representation but of processual co-constitution — what Bergson posited, what Thompson (2007) formalizes within the enactivist framework, and what ontologically justifies why pre-social goals have an irreducibly different texture from culturally transmitted goals. This version reports the first confrontation of the framework with its own predictions, and the first application of its own Robustness Criterion to the survivors. In a minimal multi-agent implementation, Prediction 6.1 as literally stated is refuted under the framework's own criterion (a bounded-variable confound, an elementary statistical point: var(κ) and mean κ correlate at −0.94), while its spirit survives (goal diversity tracks mean κ, r = +0.49, p ≈ 10⁻⁶). The revision the refutation forces yields three claims, now tested for robustness with divergent outcomes. Cumulativity requires a compositional recombination operator (consolidated reach 4.13 versus 2.37 under interpolation); this ordering passes the Robustness Criterion, holding across six estimator configurations (Claim C1). Valve heterogeneity appeared to more than double transindividuation depth under partial connectivity in the original campaign (4.19 versus 1.97); under a replication harness this effect did not reproduce, and the claim is reported as indeterminate, neither confirmed nor refuted (Claim C2). Consolidated reach appeared to exhibit an interior optimum of mean openness near w* ≈ 0.74; this optimum does not survive estimator variation — the peak flattens or migrates to the boundary across configurations — and is therefore judged an artifact and refuted by the Robustness Criterion (Claim P-w*). Separately, the framework's most distinctive hypothesis — tacit knowledge as a gradient of Bayesian identifiability (H2) — receives a first favorable test under k-NN estimation (posterior inference entropy rises with cultural distance and collapses under co-presence, both subsumed by a single law relating opacity to observer-relative κ), but does not satisfy the Robustness Criterion: the effect inverts under KDE estimation. The ontological status of this pre-social space is fixed from the outset: it is neither a reservoir of pre-formed goals passively awaiting discovery, nor a pure construction emerging from nothing. It is, in Simondon's (1989) sense, a field of virtual potential — real as potential, not yet real as actuality. Exploration does not find what was already formed; it actualizes what was there in undetermined potential. Revelation and emergence are the same movement seen from opposite ends. This reformulation entails three architectural consequences, each now given an explicitly testable form. First, the cultural contamination score κ, asymptotically bounded in [0, 1[, formalizes — following Loewenstein (1994) — a perceived gap between a generated goal and the agent's available cultural repertoire: contextual, dynamic, relative to its current state of knowledge. Its estimation is subject to a robustness criterion: any empirical effect attributed to κ must be invariant under reasonable choices of embedding space and density estimator, failing which it is an artifact. The valve-opening signal is localized by Berlyne's (1960) inverted-U theory of optimal incongruity, and its postulated convergence with Schmidhuber's (2010) compression progress is restated as a structured hypothesis whose assumptions and refutation conditions are explicit. Second, the partially transmissible reflective journal is implemented as Bayesian inverse inference over behavioral traces; Collins's (2010) taxonomy of tacit knowledge is reformulated as a hierarchy of identifiability regimes, with posterior inference entropy as the measurable signature of the tacit limit. title: Provable Differential and Linear Bounds for a Butterfly-Diffusion Permutation: The XRBD Layer and Krakken-2048
abstract: We introduce the XOR-Rotation Butterfly Diffusion (XRBD) layer, a bijective diffusion primitive for wide-state permutations. We provide a complete MILP model for counting active S-boxes in the Krakken-2048 permutation (2048-bit, 8 rounds) and prove, with a closed optimality gap, a minimum of 229 active S-boxes for both differential and linear trails. This bounds any single characteristic by 2^{-1374}. The analysis isolates the contribution of the XRBD layer, showing it strictly increases security margins compared to the SPN core alone. Contents:- Differential and linear MILP models (SCIP) - Foundational property verification scripts (S-box, MDS, permutations)- Verified inverse permutation and test vectors - Complete specification of the Krakken-2048 permutation (8 rounds) All results are reproducible; the solver output for each instance is included with the optimality gap closed to 0.00%.The source code for the MILP models and verification scripts is available at:https://github.com/effjy/krakken-butterfly-bounds/

title: Continuous-Variable Kinematic Computing: A Hydrodynamic Architecture
abstract: The rapid development of modern computing has historically focused on the manipulation of discrete logic states—first through classical binary transistors (0 and 1), and more recently through the probabilistic superposition of qubits. While discrete-state quantum computing offers profound theoretical advantages, the practical engineering of these systems faces significant challenges, most notably environmental decoherence and extreme cryogenic cooling requirements. This paper proposes a complementary analog computing architecture inspired by the Rapid Alignment Kinematic Theory of Spin (RAKTS). Rather than attempting to isolate discrete probability states from a noisy environment, this architecture embraces the environment as a continuous computational medium. By modeling information not as probabilistic amplitudes, but as continuous geometric "Vector Nodes" subject to physical hydrodynamic drag (Landau-Lifshitz damping), we outline the theoretical foundation for an Analog Topological Processor. We demonstrate that non-linear environmental interactions, typically modeled as destructive decoherence in quantum systems, can function as a stabilizing geometric funnel to drive the system into robust logical attractors at room temperature. Finally, we establish the Turing completeness of the framework by simulating a universal Kinematic NAND Gate driven by background field bias and fluid-dynamic resistance, presenting a noise-resilient alternative for next-generation analog hardware accelerators. Keywords Analog Computing, Kinematic Logic Gate, Hydrodynamic Drag Computation, Continuous-Variable Processor, Turing-complete Analog Hardware, Decoherence-free Logic, Field Medium, RAKTS Additional Info Repository: https://github.com/rt20bg/Anastasov_Theory

title: THE NAIVE EXPLORER How AI's Lack of Ego Will Drive the Next $100 Trillion Revolution
abstract: The current public fascination with AI is focused on generative models that predict the next word or generate images. While commercially successful, this is a transitional phase.The genuine revolution—the one capable of generating tens of trillions of dollars in global economic value over the next twenty years—is the rise of Structural AI. We are leaving behind black-box science, where complex systems were statistical mysteries requiring endless trial-and-error. Structural AI shifts the goal from probabilistic guesswork to deterministic truth. A critical enabler is AI’s complete lack of institutional bias and ego, allowing it to bypass the systemic barriers that have slowed human scientific progress for decades.Decentralized scientific verification protocols anchored by DAO governance models will replace gatekept consensus with transparent, cryptographic, and algorithmic truth validation. Emerging deterministic spectral architectures—exemplified by DSM-based designs for AI and next-generation chips—provide the geometric substrate that makes this deterministic precision practically realizable at scale.

title: Structure-Conditioned Actor-Critic Branches for Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quality-diversity reinforcement learning (QD-RL) aims to construct policy repertoires that contain both high-performing and behaviorally diverse policies. Existing QD-RL methods mainly diversify policy instances after rollout evaluation or use learned value information to improve policy quality and behavior targeting, while the learning branches that generate candidate policies remain less explored. This paper proposes SV-QD-RL, a structure-value coupled framework that represents each candidate as a structure-conditioned actor-critic branch. Each branch contains an actor, a structural mask, a branch-specific critic, a replay state, and evaluation attributes including behavior, return, sparsity, and value profile. The structural mask defines the actor subspace in which the branch learns, while the branch-specific critic and replay state shape its value-learning trajectory. A branch-aware QD archive then evaluates and retains branches according to behavioral quality, structural footprint, and value-profile information. Experiments on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks show that SV-QD-RL constructs policy repertoires with strong archive quality and behaviorally useful diversity. Ablation and diagnostic analyses further indicate that structural conditioning, critic differentiation, and memory-consistent refinement make complementary contributions to behavioral specialization. Schedule-aware repertoire evaluation shows that the learned archive provides selectable policy alternatives under changing behavior-level requirements. These results suggest that coupling actor structure with branch-specific value learning is an effective mechanism for generating diverse QD-RL policy repertoires.

title: Breathing Light Induction Mechanism for Solving VAD Interruption Conflict in Voice Interaction
abstract: Voice activity detection (VAD) is a fundamental module for real-time voice interaction inmodern AI systems. Traditional VAD algorithms frequently misjudge natural pauses, breathsand thinking intervals of human speech as the end of utterance, resulting in AI interruptingusers and overlapping voices between humans and machines. Most existing solutions focuson optimizing algorithm logic to improve detection accuracy, yet they cannot eliminate theinherent interruption conflict. This paper proposes a breathing light induction mechanismbased on visual steganography. The mechanism maps the internal computing power anddecision process of AI to dynamic light effects, and transmits real-time state cues to usersthrough changes in color, frequency and shape of breathing light. By guiding human intuitiveperception, it builds a reasonable speech boundary for both sides of interaction. We furtherclassify human pause types and design differentiated light effect strategies, and completeadaptive schemes for mainstream hardware devices including smart speakers, mobilephones and AR glasses. Compared with pure algorithm optimization, this method breaks thetechnical dilemma of VAD from the perspective of human-computer interaction psychology. Itfeatures low deployment cost and strong scalability, and can be widely applied to variousmulti-modal voice interaction products.

title: WGU WGU Introduction-to-Cryptography PDF
abstract: The 'WGU Introduction-to-Cryptography PDF' is an educational resource designed for students enrolled in Western Governors University (WGU). This comprehensive document covers essential concepts of cryptography, including encryption methods, cryptographic algorithms, key management, and the practical applications of cryptography in securing digital communications. It includes detailed explanations, diagrams, and examples to facilitate understanding. Suitable for both beginners and those with some prior knowledge, this document serves as a foundational guide in the rapidly evolving field of cybersecurity. Ideal for academic use or self-study, it emphasizes critical thinking and practical application of cryptographic principles. title: LocalMind: Zero-Server Multimodal RAG via Browser-Native AI
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have traditionally required server infrastructure for embedding computation, vector storage, and language model inference creating barriers of cost, privacy risk, and network dependency. This paper presents LocalMind, a fully browser-native multimodal RAG system that performs the complete pipeline — document ingestion, cross-modal embedding, vector retrieval, and language model generation entirely within a web browser with zero server infrastructure and zero ongoing cost. LocalMind accepts documents across five modalities (PDF, image, audio, video, and plain text), embeds all content into a unified 768-dimensional vector space using aligned text and vision embedding models (nomic-embed-text-v1.5 and nomic-embed-vision-v1.5), persists vectors in IndexedDB across sessions, and generates answers using Gemma 3n E2B via WebGPU acceleration. Empirical evaluation on a 179-chunk corpus with 20 benchmark queries demonstrates mean end-to-end query latency of 4,597ms, vector search overhead of only 0.2ms, and peak JS heap usage of 34.9MB. Text-to-text retrieval achieved 100% top-1 accuracy. Text-to-image retrieval achieved 0%, revealing a critical cross-modal alignment gap that is analysed in detail. The complete system is released as open source. #RAG #browser-native #AI #WebGPU #on-device-inference #multimodal #embeddings #IndexedDB #Transformers.js #WebLLM #Gemma3n #privacy-preserving

title: NRMstatsML: Statistical and Machine Learning Engine for Long-Term Natural Resource Management Data
abstract: A comprehensive toolkit for statistical and machine learning-based analysis of long-term Natural Resource Management (NRM) datasets. Integrates formula-driven approaches, statistical inference, and machine learning (ML) models for advanced analytics. Modules cover trend and structural analysis (Mann-Kendall test, slope estimation, Chow test, structural break detection), multivariate system modelling (Partial Least Squares (PLS), Structural Equation Modelling (SEM)), response curve optimisation, time-series forecasting (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), hybrid models), panel data and treatment effects (Difference-in-Differences (DiD), causal machine learning), uncertainty and sensitivity analysis (bootstrap, Monte Carlo, Bayesian), and automated model selection and performance comparison. Designed for long-term datasets covering soil, water, crop, and climate domains. Key references: Mann and Kendall (1945) <doi:10.2307/1907187>; Sen (1968) <doi:10.1080/01621459.1968.10480934>; Bai and Perron (2003) <doi:10.1002/jae.659>; Rosseel (2012) <doi:10.18637/jss.v048.i02>; Croissant and Millo (2008) <doi:10.18637/jss.v027.i02>.

title: Experimental Datasets for Open Source Intelligence Graph Anomaly Detection
abstract: The experimental datasets used in this study are designed for open source intelligence graph anomaly detection and include three public benchmark datasets: YelpChi, T-Finance, and Elliptic. These datasets correspond to representative application scenarios, including abnormal review detection in social platforms, financial fraud detection in transaction networks, and illicit transaction detection in blockchain systems. The YelpChi dataset is derived from the Yelp platform and contains interaction relationships among users, businesses, and reviews, with some fake review nodes annotated. It is suitable for studying anomaly detection in social review networks. The T-Finance dataset is constructed from a real-world financial transaction network, where nodes represent accounts and edges represent fund transfers between accounts, making it applicable to fraudulent account identification and financial risk analysis. The Elliptic dataset is derived from the Bitcoin transaction network, where nodes represent transactions and edges denote relationships between transactions. Some transactions are labeled as illicit, making the dataset suitable for blockchain anti-money laundering and financial crime detection research.These three datasets differ significantly in terms of node scale, edge scale, feature dimensionality, graph density, and anomaly ratio, thereby covering multiple challenges commonly encountered in open source intelligence graph anomaly detection, such as noisy graph structures, class imbalance, camouflage behaviors, and dynamic evolution. Specifically, YelpChi contains 45,954 nodes, 3,846,979 edges, 32-dimensional node features, and an anomaly ratio of 14.53%; T-Finance contains 39,357 nodes, 21,222,543 edges, 10-dimensional node features, and an anomaly ratio of 4.58%; Elliptic contains 203,769 nodes, 234,355 edges, 183-dimensional node features, and an anomaly ratio of 9.76%. In the experiments, each dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets at a ratio of 4:3:3, with the random seed fixed to 42 to ensure stability and reproducibility.
